title: Joins
short: Choose joins by their actual cost
lead: Every join must preserve every matching pair. Change how pages are reused, then compare the reads under explicit memory assumptions.
goals: Identify join semantics and the assumptions behind I/O calculations
Calculate the costs of tuple, page, and block nested-loop joins
Calculate index nested-loop join costs with clustering
Handle duplicates and combine the final merge pass with a sort-merge join

sections.title: Produce every matching pair without rereading so much
sections.html:
We have Student(id,name)=[(7,An),(9,Bình)] and Enrolment(id,course)=[(7,DB),(7,AI),(8,OS)]. To attach course names to students, compare IDs. An matches both DB and AI, so emit (7,An,DB) and (7,An,AI); Bình matches none. This original inner-join example shows what every algorithm must preserve: all matching pairs, not one result per key. A nested loop implements that directly: choose a Student row, inspect all Enrolment rows, then choose the next Student row. The side driving the repeated loop is the outer input; the repeatedly searched side is the inner input.

The waste appears when the inner input cannot stay in memory: each new outer row can trigger another full inner scan. Since reading one outer page already brought several rows into RAM, compare all of them during a single inner scan. Better still, retain several outer pages as a block. The condition can be arbitrary; these loop methods do not require equality.

Now count with a larger original example: R has M=120 pages and m=12,000 tuples; S has N=40 pages; B=12 one-page frames. Inputs are nonempty. Count reads, ignore CPU and final-output writes, and assume the inner file is not retained across scans. Reserve one inner frame and one output frame, leaving B−2=10 outer frames.

Method, R outerWhat causes one S scan?Page I/Os
Tuple nested loopsEach of 12,000 outer tuples120+12,000×40=480,120
Page nested loopsEach of 120 outer pages120+120×40=4,920
Block nested loopsEach of ceil(120/10)=12 outer blocks120+12×40=600

For block 1, read R pages 1…10, keep them while scanning S pages 1…40, emit every matching pair, then replace the block with R pages 11…20 and scan S again. Repeating this twelve times reads R once, 120 pages, and S twelve times, 480 pages. Hence M+ceil(M/(B−2))N. The ceiling rounds up because an incomplete last block still scans all S. Reverse the roles: S outer gives 40+ceil(40/10)×120=520. Calculate both orientations; rounding affects the answer. If the outer fits one block, each input is read once, M+N.

Key takeaway

Use the number of outer blocks to count inner scans. With 12 frames, the outer block uses 10 frames. Each outer block triggers one complete read of the inner input.

sections.title: Use an inner index to replace a full scan
sections.html:
In the small example, probing an Enrolment index for Student ID 7 should return both DB and AI. Stopping at the first match changes the join answer. An index nested-loop join reads each outer tuple, extracts its join key and looks up every corresponding inner tuple. The index must support that condition: an equality-capable index can support id equality, but its existence says nothing about an unrelated predicate.

Suppose filtering leaves 25 outer tuples on two pages. One inner unique-key lookup costs three page reads in total, including the index path and the fetched data row. First read the two outer pages. Then perform 25 probes: 25×3=75 reads. Total=2+75=77 I/Os. In general use M+m×C_lookup, where M is outer pages, m is outer tuples and C_lookup includes all inner matches. If probe costs differ by key, sum them or choose a justified average. To isolate probe count, hold the outer read cost at two and imagine 2,500 probes: 2+2,500×3=7,502. This comparison deliberately fixes outer read cost; it is not a claim that every 2,500-row relation uses two pages.

Why might one probe cost more than three? A nonunique key can span several leaf pages and many data pages. With a clustered index, matching rows may share a few pages; with an unclustered one, each may require a separate cold fetch. A warm index root may lower navigation reads, but does not by itself cache all referenced records. The calculation must distinguish index access, record fetches and the number of matching tuples.

A probe finds three inner matches on two data pages. May it count one fetch because the join key was found once?

Reasoned answer. No. It must produce all three pairs and fetch the two necessary pages under a cold-cache model, plus uncached index reads. One matching key value is not the same unit as one result row or one data page.

Key takeaway

A lookup must account for every match. An index does not automatically make a join cheap: cost also depends on the number of outer tuples, the number of matches, and the data pages that must be read.

sections.title: Bring equal keys together with sorting or hashing
sections.html:
The repeated inner scans can also be avoided by organising both inputs. For a sort-merge equijoin, sort each by join key, then compare the current keys. In original sorted keys R=[2,7,7,9], S=[1,7,7,7,10], compare 2 with 1 and advance S; compare 2 with 7 and advance R. Both now show 7. Do not advance both after emitting one pair: there are two R occurrences and three S occurrences.

R: r1=7, r2=7
S: s1=7, s2=7, s3=7
R ⋈ S: (r1,s1), (r1,s2), (r1,s3),
      (r2,s1), (r2,s2), (r2,s3)

Buffer and reuse a group that fits. If duplicate groups require spilling or rescanning, add that work. Once the 7 groups are consumed, compare 9 with 10, advance R to its end and stop. With duplicate handling that needs no extra reads, already sorted inputs cost M+N scan reads. If complete sorted files are first written to disk, total=sort(R)+sort(S)+M+N. The lecture’s extreme duplicate case describes a rescan strategy; it is not a universal implementation cost.

An in-memory hash equijoin instead builds a hash table from one input, keeping needed tuples including duplicate occurrences, then probes with the other. Build=[r1=7,r2=7]; each of three s rows with key 7 produces two pairs, again six. Compare actual keys to reject hash collisions. The build table, overhead and input/output buffers must fit RAM. The probe side can stream; then reading each input once costs M+N. A key occurring a million times cannot generally be collapsed into a SUM state without changing an ordinary join’s output.

When the build does not fit, Grace hash join partitions both inputs by the same key hash so matching keys reach paired partitions R_i,S_i. For each pair, build on the smaller fitting partition and probe with the other, using a suitable independent hash distinction within it. Count all input reads M+N, partition writes M+N and partition rereads M+N: 3(M+N). For our 120+40 pages, this is 480 I/Os, excluding result writes, if no extra partitioning is needed. Oversized pairs need recursive repartitioning and more I/O; identical-key skew cannot be split by rehashing and needs a fallback preserving every pair. Large many-to-many results still consume real CPU and output bandwidth even when a comparison model excludes result writes.

sections.title: Save a write/read cycle only when buffers permit it
sections.html:
Why finish writing sorted files just to reread them for a merge join? Their last sorting pass can feed the join directly. But both final merges need their input runs available together. Let r and s be the remaining run counts just before the final pass. In the basic fused model, reserve one frame per run and one join-output frame; require r+s≤B−1. Duplicate handling must need no additional spill space or rescans. “Each input sorts in two passes” alone does not establish this combined fit.

Our R=120, S=40B=12B=16
Initial R runs ceil(120/B)108
Initial S runs ceil(40/B)43
Combined run inputs1411
Available after output frame1115
Fuse these unchanged two-pass sorts?No: 14>11Yes: 11≤15, with stated duplicate assumptions

At B=16, pass 0 reads and writes all 160 pages: 2×160=320 I/Os. The fused pass reads the runs once: 160 more. Total=480, excluding join-output writes. Materialising each two-pass sort costs 2×160×2=640, then rereading sorted files for join adds 160: 800. Fusion saves 320, one write and one read of the two inputs. At B=12 the original 14-run arrangement does not fit; use extra merging or another allocation and count its cost. If an input already supplies the required order, do not charge an unnecessary sort, and do not assume those sorted pages are cached.

For 120 and 40 pages with twelve frames, compare the best block nested loop, two-phase Grace hash and a merge of already sorted inputs. Then change the join condition to an inequality.

Reasoned answer. Block nested loops: min(600,520)=520. Grace: 480 only if each build partition and overhead fit, with suitable distribution. Already-sorted merge: 160 scan reads if duplicate handling adds none. An inequality invalidates the equality-based hash calculation; nested loops still applies. Required output order, existing indexes, cache and result size can change the choice. These estimates compare explicitly stated plans, not universal rankings.

Use the join-cost lab to swap outer and inner and explain the changed block count before looking at the total. Its sort-merge row materialises sort outputs; the fused case above is a separate plan. A hash-feasibility warning means the displayed two-phase estimate cannot describe execution under that model.

quiz.question: Two groups with the same key contain 3 and 4 tuples. How many joined tuples do they produce?
quiz.explanation: Pair each of the three first-input occurrences with all four second-input occurrences: 4+4+4=12 output tuples. A join does not deduplicate the groups. Sorting or hashing can organise the comparisons differently, but cannot discard any of these valid pairs.
